title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up.

title: Apple's 'Reference Image' Preserves Your Original Photos (Even After You Edit Them)
description: Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple int
body:
Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple introduced a new standard to at least help identify real images taken directly on an iPhone: Apple Reference Image. It won’t solve the problem of finding the truth online, but it could be a helpful tool towards that goal.The new feature will be available on iPhone 18 Pro models to start. It works by taking signed sensor data from the camera and using it to create a reference picture that can’t be edited, alongside a version that can be changed. The idea here is to give you a version of the picture that’s authenticated at the moment of capture, which you can compare against any modified versions later.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Credit: Apple
                    
    
This provenance metadata can be preserved through certain supported sharing methods, which for now means select other Apple devices can check their verification status. That doesn’t mean that anyone can check the veracity of an image—especially if the version that gets posted and shared is an edited variant—but it provides a tool for the person or organization that took the picture originally to offer proof of verification.
This tool comes alongside the announcement that Apple will soon add support for the SynthID standard. This will potentially help users identify when an image has been created or modified with AI. Apple joins a long (though not exactly comprehensive) list of major tech companies to support the standard, including OpenAI, Nvidia, and obviously Google, the original creator of SynthID.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We’re still in the midst of a scattershot image verification ecosystem. Apple’s Reference Image is a clever implementation that gives the end user a signed original to compare a picture against, which is a step up from C2PA metadata that merely embeds information about an image’s origin. It’s still unclear how widely these verification tools will be implemented and how easy it will be for users to trace where an image comes from and how, precisely, it was modified, but still, something is better than nothing.

body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

            Credit: Robert Way via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.

title: Over 150 Million Driver's Licenses Have Been Leaked
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 11, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Yeong-Ung Yang/Newsday via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            If you have a driver's license in the U.S or Canada, there's a pretty good chance that your data was stolen.
                                            A massive hack at ID verification company IDScan.net compromised records for more than 150 million drivers.
                                            Be on the lookout for a notice from IDScan.net.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you have a driver's license in the U.S or Canada, there's a pretty good chance that your data was recently for sale on the dark web. A massive hack at ID verification company IDScan.net compromised records for more than 150 million drivers, resulting in scans of licenses being made available to bad actors. IDScan.net is a Louisiana-based company that provides identity and age verification services for industries ranging from casinos and cannabis dispensaries to hotels and car rentals. What happened with the IDScan.net breach?According to an incident notice on IDScan's website, the company received information "on or around" Sept. 1 that an unauthorized third party was able to gain access to stored customer data, including full names along with driver's license and government-issued ID numbers. This was around the time that a major breach was reported by cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs, who received a tip that driver's license information—including digital scans—was available for sale on the dark web via an identity theft service dubbed Nexus. The platform advertised access to more than 153 million driver's licenses, and Krebs and security researcher Zach Edwards verified the data and identified IDScan as the likely source. As TechCrunch reports, the FBI is investigating the breach, and the database has since been taken offline. 
What to do if your drivers license has been compromisedA lost or stolen driver's license creates a high risk of identity theft and fraud, as hackers can use it to open financial accounts and take out loans in your name, commit mail fraud, create a fake ID, and even develop a synthetic identity (which combines both real and fake personal data) that could be used to commit a crime. If thieves have access to your physical license or a scan, as in this latest breach, they have a complete set of information, including your birth date and photo, to assume your identity. Fraudsters can also do a lot of damage with just your driver's license number. If your driver's license information has been compromised in a breach, you should take all the usual steps against identity theft, including pulling your credit reports, monitoring your financial accounts, and setting up fraud alerts. (At this point in the data breach game, your credit should already be frozen unless you are actively applying for a new card or loan, but if you haven't yet, do it immediately.) 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Because your driver's license is so valuable to identity thieves, Experian also recommends requesting your driving record, which you can get from your state's department of motor vehicles, and running a background check on yourself. Both can reveal if any fraudulent activities have been carried out in your name—for example, if someone has been pulled over or if there are arrest warrants or criminal charges linked to your identity. You can file a police report for a lost or stolen license and report identity theft if you believe your information is being used fraudulently. IDScan.net is reportedly alerting individuals affected by this latest breach, and given its scale, you should be on the lookout for a notice. The company is offering credit monitoring and identity protection services to those impacted, and you can call 1-833-516-2980 to enroll.

        Nintendo announced the new The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time at its Nintendo Direct event this week. And already, Walmart has the game available for $59.99 (originally $69.99) for pre-order. Judging by how fast other pre-orders for the new remake have been going since the announcement, I wouldn't be surprised if this pre-order deal sells out too. And you're unlikely to see another discount on this major Nintendo game like the one Walmart is offering.
The Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition console does not come with the game, so you will have to buy a physical or digital copy separately. Nintendo announced that the first printing of physical copies would include a "textured foil cover art" while supplies last, but it's unclear whether this sale is for that version. No pre-order product page lists whether it's a foil version, but as long as you're pre-ordering, you improve your chances of being in that pool.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The game will release on Nov. 5, and it's a faithful remake of the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time with improved graphics, cutscenes with dialogue, new mechanics (Link can jump now), and other new additions. It would be inaccurate to call it a one-to-one remake. I'm hoping Nintendo finally gives us the Light Temple that the original game on the N64 could not fit in the game. We'll just have to find out on Nov. 5, when the game releases.

It's meant for quick setups, like putting on a movie in your living room or taking it out to a terrace, and it's on sale for just $64.99 on StackSocial right now. This is the original 2017 model, not the OLED version, so the display and battery are a step behind newer revisions. Even so, it delivers the same core idea: you can take your games anywhere. Its 6.2-inch touchscreen is sharp enough for everyday play, and the system is small enough to toss into a bag without thinking.Using the Switch feels simple. You might start a game on the TV, then pull it out of the dock and keep playing from the couch or in bed without thinking much about it. Set it on a table, and the kickstand lets you prop it up for a quick match with a friend using the Joy-Cons separately. Those controllers are part of what makes it work so well. They attach to the sides when you want a handheld, or you can use them on their own without buying extras right away. Motion controls add another layer for games that support them (though not every title uses them well). And, as for its battery life, it ranges from about 4.5 to 9 hours, depending on the game, so lighter titles last longer, while more demanding ones will drain it faster.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
This is a refurbished unit with a Grade-A rating, so it should arrive close to brand new. Games aren't included, and storage is modest unless you add a microSD card, so you will need to budget for those separately. The original Switch obviously doesn't match the graphics or speed of the Switch 2, but the price is right, and you can still move between handheld, tabletop, and TV mode without changing setups, which makes it a practical choice for casual gaming, travel, or sharing quick sessions with friends.

title: iPhones Are Getting More Expensive, but AirPods Are Cheaper Than Ever
body:
Khamosh Pathak
                            
        
            Khamosh Pathak
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceKhamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is increasing the price of all existing iPhone models, including iPhone 17e, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17.
                                            The newly released AirPods 5 are actually cheaper than the outgoing model.
                                            The Apple Watch series has surprisingly missed the price bump.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        RAMageddon is real, and it’s finally come for the iPhone. Thanks to the ever-increasing costs of memory and storage, the prices of virtually all tech products are going up. A couple of months ago, Apple increased the pricing for the Mac and the iPad, by a couple of hundred dollars. Now, it’s the iPhone’s turn: Suddenly, all the iPhones are now $100 more expensive than they were yesterday, and the newly announced models are $100 more expensive than last year. But it’s not all doom and gloom. The new AirPods are actually cheaper, and mercifully, some Apple products remain the same price.The $100 iPhone bump
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
At the September keynote event, Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256GB storage, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is now $1,399. Both of them are $100 more than the starting price of comparable iPhone 17 Pro/Max models.
The price bump doesn't stop with the new phones: Apple has flipped a switch and bumped prices on all existing iPhone models by $100. While Apple did not introduce an iPhone 18, the price of the iPhone 17 has quietly gone up; it now starts at $899 for the 256GB model instead of $799. The older iPhone 16 model is now $799, while the "budget" iPhone 17e now sells for $699. Even the iPhone Air has gone up to $1099.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple Watch pricing stays the sameSurprisingly, the RAM and storage costs haven’t hit the Apple Watch yet, or, at least, Apple is willing to absorb those increases for these smaller devices. The Series 12 Apple Watch with a new S11 processor and on-device Apple Intelligence features starts at the same $399 price as the Apple Watch 11. The new Apple Watch Ultra 4 also remains at the same $799 introductory price as the Ultra 3.AirPods are now cheaper (and better) than everOne popular product escaped the price bump: I was surprised to see a new standard AirPods model at the iPhone 18 Pro keynote, but the price drop was even more unexpected. The base AirPods 5 now come with built-in ANC (which used to cost extra), along with better transparency and improved sound features, and they are just $129, the cost of the outgoing AirPods 4 without ANC. Apple does have a more expensive model of AirPods 5 that comes with a wireless charging case, better battery life, and an on-stem voice control feature for $149, or $30 cheaper than the outgoing AirPods 4 with ANC model.

title: Microsoft's Record-Setting Patch Tuesday Update Fixes Nearly 1,000 Flaws
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July.
                                            Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild.
                                            AI is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities as well as allowing developers to fix them more quickly.
                                            It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Security updates have been trending larger, and Microsoft's Patch Tuesday for September is no exception. The company just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July (the previous record). Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild. This massive jump is in large part due to AI, which is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities while also allowing developers to find and fix them more quickly. This means we're likely to continue seeing sizeable updates on shorter release cycles, ideally reducing the time hackers have to take advantage of these flaws. Microsoft has typically pushed Patch Tuesday fixes around 10 a.m. PT on the second Tuesday of every month. It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation. PC users should receive Patch Tuesday updates automatically, but you can check the status via Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates.
September's Patch Tuesday addresses 966 flaws with two zero-days As BleepingComputer reports, the 966 flaws fixed this month are broken down across the following categories: 438 elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, 19 security feature bypass vulnerabilities, 258 remote-code-execution vulnerabilities, 173 information disclosure vulnerabilities, 16 spoofing vulnerabilities, and 56 denial-of-service vulnerabilities. These figures do not include other vulnerabilities (204 in total across other Microsoft products) patched earlier this month. One of the zero-days addressed in September is an elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Windows Update Stack. CVE-2026-81963 allows attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges via improper link resolution before file access. The bug discovery has been attributed to Romain Deperne and the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Centre. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The other zero-day is also an elevation of privilege vulnerability. CVE-2026-85880 is a flaw in the Windows Advanced Local Procedure—an attacker could execute code in a low-privilege AppContainer, and the vulnerability could escape the sandbox and gain SYSTEM privileges locally. The bug was discovered by Volexity, as well as Mark Kelly, David Galazin, and Jeremy Hedges with Proofpoint. Both zero-days have been actively exploited in the wild, though Microsoft has not provided any details as to how.

title: Here's Why You Should Care About the iPhone 18 Pro's 'Vapor Chambers'
description: During Apple’s big hardware announcement on Wednesday, the company placed a particular emphasis on the vapor chamber in the new iPho
body:
During Apple’s big hardware announcement on Wednesday, the company placed a particular emphasis on the vapor chamber in the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The glossed-over explanation is that these new vapor chambers can improve performance and reduce heat generation. But how exactly? And what does that mean for the phones you’re planning to buy?How vapor chambers workOn a very simple level, vapor chambers work similarly to liquid cooling in other electronics systems like some desktop PCs or server racks. The goal is to carry heat away from the processor to keep it cool, so it can do more work without overheating. A cooler processor is a more efficient processor, which means it runs better.Except, unlike a PC or server rack, a phone is a tight, compact system. There’s not enough space to heat water and then pump it away to a different location to cool it down. Instead, a vapor chamber is a thin, hollow chamber, typically made of either copper or stainless steel, with a small amount of liquid inside. When the liquid inside heats up, it becomes a gas, which then expands outwards, dispersing the heat throughout the body of your phone, rather than keeping it all close to the processor. As it gets further away from the source of heat, the vapor cools back down and becomes a liquid again.
Since the chamber is sealed, the liquid can’t evaporate and escape, meaning that the fluid can theoretically keep cycling through the chamber indefinitely for the life of the phone. Most manufacturers also pair this with some form of heat sink, like thin sheets of graphite or copper. Or, in the case of the new iPhone 18 Pro, both.Why vapor chambers matter for smartphonesKeeping your phone cool is a massive problem compared to other electronic devices you might have, simply because they’re so small, yet so powerful. A moderately powered laptop like a MacBook Air can get away with a combination of conductive heat sinks, a metal frame, and low heat-generating processors to stay functional, while high-powered gaming laptops have space to stuff in large, laborious fans.Your phone, however, needs to fit in your pocket, and a huge chunk of the space inside needs to be devoted to the battery to make sure it lasts long enough to get through the day. Once you account for all the processors, sensors, and antennas that a phone needs, there’s scarcely any space left for heat dissipation. That’s a huge part of why phones generally don’t have as powerful processors as tablets or laptops. Physically, it’s not impossible to fit a high-powered chip in a pocketable device. But it would likely generate so much heat that it would destroy itself without proper heat dissipation, which would make your phone too big for a pocket.This kind of heat dissipation matters even more if you happen to live in places with warm climates. For example, I live in Texas. Even when driving inside an air-conditioned car, if my phone is in the sunlight, it can start to overheat. When I previously had a Pixel 6 Pro, it would occasionally shut off (taking my navigation with it) simply because it wasn’t in the shade. After upgrading to a Pixel 9 Pro, which does have a vapor chamber, I never noticed this problem—though this is obviously anecdotal.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to consider vapor chambers when buying a phoneApple says the iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the previous generation, which theoretically should mean better cooling and, thus, better performance. But does that mean you need to decide what phone to buy based on how big a phone’s vapor chamber is, or whether it has one at all?Well, yes and no. It turns out that outside the Apple ecosystem, Android phones have been using vapor chambers for years, and you might not have even noticed. The existence of vapor chambers is increasingly becoming standard, so unless you have an old phone that frequently overheats, or you’re looking to buy a phone a few generations behind, you probably don’t need to go out of your way to make sure your phone has one.And whether bigger is necessarily better is also a bit of a gray area. All other things being equal, yes, a larger vapor chamber will dissipate heat better and keep your phone cooler. But all other things are rarely equal. A larger vapor chamber also means the manufacturer can put a more powerful processor inside and achieve the same thermal balance. So, a phone could theoretically be equally likely to overheat, but do more before it does.Figuring out the right balance between processing power and heat dissipation is the kind of thing best left to the engineers and dedicated hobbyists. But there are a couple of things the average person can take away from this. First, if you live in a warm climate, better heat dissipation is always going to be better. Your phone isn’t running at full power all day, but the Texas sun is. So, if you’re worried about your environment causing overheating problems, check phone reviews for how well it handles heat. More importantly, consider the power needs you have for your device before you buy. If you just use your phone to scroll TikTok and reply to emails, you probably don’t need an overpowered processor, but if you plan to edit 4K videos or play graphically intense mobile games, then better thermal regulation could do you some good.

title: Apple Just Announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple/YouTube
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple officially announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max on Wednesday.
                                            The new iPhones look like the previous generation, the iPhone 17 Pro, but have smaller Dynamic Islands and come in new colors.
                                            The iPhone 18 Pro series also comes with variable apertures for the first time on iPhone, which will improve light control and bokeh.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The iPhone Duo will inevitably steal tech headlines this week. After all, Apple finally made a foldable iPhone to compete with options from Samsung and Google. But while an iPhone with two displays is novel and exciting, it's also going to be expensive. I imagine there are many in the market for a new iPhone who aren't interested in spending as much as $2,000. There are also likely customers who don't want a foldable iPhone, and would prefer the standard smartphone design they're used to. That's where the iPhone 18 Pro comes in. iPhone 18 Pro: DesignIf you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you might confuse it for the iPhone 18 Pro. Indeed, Apple hasn't changed the overall design much this year, which is to be expected. The iPhone 17 Pro refreshed the Pro iPhone design with its large camera bump and plane of glass for MagSafe charging. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't much different—though now the metal is color-matched to the back glass.That being said, there are some changes here you may notice upon closer examination. Perhaps first you'd notice the 18 Pro's Dynamic Island is smaller than it has been on previous Pro iPhones. With it, you're able to run three tasks at once, rather than two. That may prove useful depending on what you're doing, or it may end up cluttering the top of your iPhone. 18 Pro users will have to be the judge. You'd also notice some new color options not available on the iPhone 17 Pro, which I'll cover below.    
The displays will remain the same sizes as last year—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro, and 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But now, these displays use a more efficient LPTO+ technology. iPhone 18 Pro: ProcessorLike the iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pros come with Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology. The company touts how the new chip is great for processing AI on-device, with a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, new Neural Accelerators, and a second Neural Engine. Apple focused on the A20 Pro's thermal cooling with the new vapor chamber in the 18 Pro. Apple says this means there are significant sustained performance improvements over the iPhone 17 Pro.    Apple says this chip has the fastest CPU in a smartphone, with 50% better memory bandwidth. But, as with all performance claims, we'll have to wait until testers try out the A20 Pro for themselves. Still, Apple's newest chips always improve on the previous generation by some degree, so it's safe to say the 18 Pro (and the Duo at that) will be the fastest iPhones yet. Apple also says the iPhone 18 Pro has 36 hours of battery life while streaming video, while iPhone 18 Pro Max has 45 hours. The company says five minutes of charging gets you six hours of video playback.   iPhone 18 Pro: CamerasPerhaps the biggest change for the iPhone 18 Pro this year is its cameras. Apple's Pro iPhones are known for their shooters, but for the 18 Pros, Apple has taken things up a notch. For the first time, these iPhones have variable apertures. When using the 48MP main camera, your iPhone can physically open and close its aperture to control how much light hits the sensor—up to 50% more light than before. That offers two benefits: In dim environments, you can let in more light than you normally could. You can also use the aperture to control the depth of field, or the background blur. A large aperture (more light) means a blurrier background, while a smaller aperture (less light) means a cleaner background. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple also introduced Pro Controls, which has been sorely missing on the iPhone. You now can control white balance and shutter speed, and check the histogram. This mode works for both photography and videography. There's now a new "smart focus tracking" feature that uses AI to keep focus on a subject. Photographic Styles get some additional upgrades and controls, and Time-Lapse also supports 4K. With the 18 Pro, Apple is rolling out a "reference" feature to ensure that an original shot can be confirmed if an edit is later made with AI. Apple calls this a "digital negative." iPhone 18 Pro: ColorsAs previously mentioned, the iPhone 18 Pro's colors may be one of the most recognisably "new" features of this generation. Apple is rolling out color options in "Burgundy," "Glacier," and Silver, though the first two may be the more distinct of the bunch. Still, it's more variation than we have on the Duo.iPhone 18 Pro: PriceEverything is getting more expensive, thanks to RAMaggedon, and the iPhone 18 Pro is no exception. Apple is raising the starting price this year to $1,199 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for the 256GB variant. iPhone 18 Pro: Release dateApple says the iPhone 18 Pro will be available to preorder on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12 a.m. PT (3 a.m. ET). The devices then go on sale Friday, Sept. 18.

These are all pre-recorded courses with lifetime access, so they work best for self-paced learners who are comfortable navigating different instructors and formats—that can be both a strength and a drawback, so this great deal makes the most sense if you're planning to spend real time learning or building projects.
